title: Recent gigs and playing for patients at Charity Hospital
summary: He played with Papa French and then for hospital patients; a woman recovered a song, showing what music means to people.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Other than the other night. I played Joe Gordon. I played with him with Papa Celestine.
I mean Papa French. We played a job for him out of Madrid. And we had a nice time out there. It was wonderful. What year was that? That was, uh, that was about a month ago or two months ago.

And we had a lovely time out there. And they had two other fellas. One could play piano and the other one could play ghetto. But the other fella, he didn't want to play. I sang about three numbers. And, uh, every time I looked around, there was some ladies, you know, would come up, ask the same, sing the same number. Then another lady, she would take up a number herself. Well, it's good when you can, uh, catch someone to sing. And while they're singing, you know just what chord to hit the chord chord with them. You know what I mean? That's a great thing. And, uh, now, a lot of people don't know what music is. But it's the greatest thing in the world. You know what amused me one night? We played what you call projects sometimes. And we played at the, uh, at the Charity Hospital on the third floor. And that was last year I played there. And it was so amusing to see. That's what tell you what music is. You take some people, they'll get, say the blues, or they get down and out, and they'll get up, they'll find, they'll hear a number on a music box. And they'll sit there, and maybe you say to yourself, you live here in the head and a little drink. I'm tired of hearing that number. I'm tired of hearing that number. Well, this guy, he's right there. And every time that number stops, he's playing it right back. Well, that's amusing him. Now, on this third floor, we played about four numbers. And another number we played. And here, from one of those, uh, ladies, she came up. And she started singing that number. And when she started singing the number, the nurses and the doctors, they come up by the band. And, uh, doctor, he came around. She said, you know, so, yeah. When you stop, she said, play that number again, please. She played that number over. She came back. Now, I don't know her name, but she said she used to sing those numbers on Burlington Street. She had a snap, you understand, on the third floor, and never forget it. That's what made me, too, know how much music means to people. And just like we played at the veteran hospital, at the marine hospitals, and we played for those people, the vocal from New York, you know, picture your name and send you to those different places. And, uh, it's amusing. People wouldn't imagine how much music means. Now, when we played on that third floor, I don't know whether... That brought back a little touch of reality to that woman's phone number. That's right. It brought back to her. And, uh, now whether she kept going along or whether she were, you know, uh, fell back, I don't know. But, uh, I was telling the guys in the band, I said, man, I said, you know, and I said, you see where that lady... Uh, she was thinking about numbers that she... by playing at one number. And then she began to ask for this for different numbers. And those doctors, I mean, it just had been...
You had done something they couldn't do. They couldn't...

Yeah, yeah. And, uh, they came up and they just talked with me, and, uh, Julie should know any numbers, any other numbers. Well, some other numbers we played. It's hard to think right off, you know, and so some other numbers we played. And, uh, she sang a little part of that. She couldn't get all the numbers of that, but it was so nice to know that her mind had come back to that number, you know. But that other number... Right.

She sang it all the way through twice. And she went on off, humming her number to herself. Doctor said, I wish I could keep you all here all night. He said, you might do something else. So the doctor did ask for my band back the next time. You see, because on six and six at one birthday, I was up there on the third floor. No, not all of them because there was one night one of them come and took my mic. And the guy said, Julius, I said, what?
What was he going to do with it?
Julius, she got your mic. I said, she can have it.

So a nurse came up. She said, what's the matter? I said, she had my mic. She said, oh, I'll get it for you. I said, thank you. I said, Andy, why didn't you go get it? I said, who, she could have that mic. I wasn't going up there. I mean, I wasn't poking fun, but I mean, I was afraid of them. And I wasn't going up there to prove it no mic.
